name: Keawanui shore fishpond
summary: Keawanui, a Hawaiian shore fishpond on Molokaʻi enclosed by a stone seawall, where marine fish were raised and managed under chiefly control.
description: Keawanui’s enclosed coastal fishpond on Molokaʻi, with a stone seawall and managed marine fish culture.
tier_reason: A bounded technical contribution, transmission episode or documented configuration useful within a specific history; no broad dependence claim is established.

impact.note: One pond among many supplying one community with managed fish, with nothing later known to rest on it; implies tier 3, below the reviewed tier 2.

why: Enclosing shallow reef flats let communities keep a dependable supply of fish close at hand.

date.label: by c. 1600 CE (inferred)
date.basis: NPS dates pond construction to around 1575 and describes operation; by c.1600 is an approximate contextual horizon, not a precise commissioning date.

events.statement: The Keawanui enclosed pond was operated in the local managed-fishery setting.
events.population: Keawanui pond keepers and the chiefly controlled local community
events.caveats: Construction is approximate and initial use is inferred; chiefly control and unequal access are not generalized into common ownership. Later restoration is separate.

evidence.supports: NPS identifies the chief-associated shore pond, seawall, approximate construction date and later operation.

date.basis: The date applies to this particular documented event or period, not to the origin of the practice.

events.statement: Hui o Kuapā – Keawanui Fishpond, formerly the Hawaiian Learning Center, restored and maintained Keawanui from 1999 and later used the pond for education.

evidence.supports: The report describes Hui o Kuapā – Keawanui Fishpond, formerly known as the Hawaiian Learning Center, restoring and maintaining Keawanui since 1999 and using the site for education. It is based on community-engagement work and does not date original construction.

events.caveats: The community report gives 1999 as the start of this work; other sources describe earlier wider fishpond-revival efforts.

events.statement: After a tsunami damaged the pond wall, community members began repairs; a local practitioner also reported an oyster harvest by students.

evidence.supports: Ritte reports about fifty people contributing to restoration after the 2011 tsunami and students at Ho‘omana Hou School harvesting 34 pounds of oysters. The latter is one reported harvest, not annual yield or proof of continuous production.

events.caveats: The practitioner reported repairs in progress and one harvest; the account does not establish completion of all wall repairs or annual production.
